slides.title: From ERC-20 to ERC-721
slides.intro: ERC-20 introduced token standards: if everyone follows the same standard, wallets, exchanges, smart contracts and applications already know how to interact with the token.
points: Today: another extremely important Ethereum token standard — ERC-721
ERC-721 is commonly known as the NFT standard
NFT stands for Non-Fungible Token
Before we write any code, we need to understand what non-fungible actually means

callout.text: ERC-20 → every token is equivalent.   ERC-721 → every token is unique.

slides.title: Fungible vs Non-Fungible
slides.subtitle: What makes one token different from another?

left.heading: ERC-20 — Fungible
items: Alice's 1 token = Bob's 1 token = John's 1 token
One token is equivalent to another token of the same type
We only count how many units each address holds

right.heading: ERC-721 — Non-Fungible
items: Every token can represent something unique
Each token has its own token ID
We track who owns each individual token

slides.title: Unique Things in the Real World

cards.title: Houses
cards.text: Same price — still two different houses

cards.title: Concert Tickets
cards.text: Each ticket is for a different seat

cards.title: Game Items
cards.text: Each sword is its own item

callout.text: That's the basic idea of an NFT: one token represents one specific, unique item.

slides.title: What Actually Makes an NFT Unique?
slides.intro: A common beginner misunderstanding: an NFT is simply an image. That's not correct — the token identifies ownership, and the image and other information usually live in metadata referenced by the token.

callout.text: The important concepts are token ID, ownership and metadata.

slides.title: Token IDs & Ownership
slides.subtitle: balanceOf  •  ownerOf  •  the core ERC-721 functions

slides.title: Token IDs — Every NFT Has Its Own Number
points: `uint256 tokenId;` identifies each individual NFT
Token #1, #2, #3, #4 — each one is a separate asset
Alice can own multiple NFTs (#1 and #3)
But token #1 itself has one owner at a time

slides.title: balanceOf — ERC-20 vs ERC-721

left.heading: ERC-20
items: Tells us how many fungible units Alice owns

right.heading: ERC-721
items: Tells us how many different NFTs Alice owns
`ownerOf` tells us which specific NFTs are hers

slides.source: OpenZeppelin Docs — the ERC-721 implementation exposes ownership, balances, approvals and safe transfers.

slides.title: Core ERC-721 Functions

cards.title: balanceOf(owner)
cards.text: How many NFTs an address owns

cards.title: safeTransferFrom(...)
cards.text: Moves an NFT and checks the receiver can accept it

cards.title: approve(...)
cards.text: Lets one address transfer one NFT: `(to, tokenId)`

cards.title: getApproved(...)
cards.text: Which address is approved for a token: `(tokenId)`

cards.title: setApprovalForAll(...)
cards.text: Lets an operator manage all your NFTs: `(operator, true)`

slides.source: OpenZeppelin Docs — ERC-721 core functionality: ownership, balances, approvals and safe transfers.

left.heading: balanceOf(address)
items: Alice owns NFT #1, #4 and #8
`balanceOf(Alice) = 3`

right.heading: ownerOf(tokenId)
items: Asks about one specific NFT
`ownerOf(8) → Alice`

slides.title: NFT Ownership Internally — the Concept

blocks.label: Learning model only — not production code

points: Conceptually, NFT ownership is a mapping: token ID → owner
A second mapping can track how many NFTs each address holds
You already know mappings, so you can understand what an NFT ownership system is trying to achieve

callout.text: In production we do not implement ERC-721 ourselves like this. We look at the concept so we understand what OpenZeppelin does for us.

slides.title: MyNFT — Your First ERC-721 Contract
points: `import` — reuse OpenZeppelin's ERC-721 instead of writing the standard ourselves
`is ERC721` — MyNFT inherits the whole standard
`constructor` — passes the collection name and symbol to the parent
`nextTokenId` — a counter that gives every NFT a new ID
`_safeMint(to, tokenId)` — creates the NFT and assigns its owner

callout.label: REMIX
callout.text: OpenZeppelin 5.x needs compiler 0.8.24 or newer — select it in the Solidity Compiler tab.

slides.source: OpenZeppelin Docs — widely used implementations of standards such as ERC-20 and ERC-721.

slides.title: Inheritance & Constructor
points: You now see why we learned inheritance before token standards
MyNFT inherits the `ERC721` contract
The parent `ERC721` constructor needs the collection name and symbol

slides.title: Minting — Creating a New NFT
points: Minting creates the NFT and assigns ownership
`nextTokenId++` makes sure every new NFT gets a fresh ID

slides.title: Live Demo in Remix — MyNFT
points: Compile with 0.8.24 or newer, then deploy `MyNFT` using Account 1
Call `mint(Account1)` — paste Account 1's address
Call `ownerOf(0)` → returns Account 1
Call `balanceOf(Account1)` → returns 1
Mint another NFT, then call `balanceOf(Account1)` → returns 2

callout.text: The address owns two NFTs, while each NFT has its own token ID (0 and 1).

slides.title: Why _safeMint and Not Just mint?
slides.intro: The safe version provides additional protection when an NFT is minted to another smart contract.
points: If the receiver is a smart contract, ERC-721 verifies that it knows how to accept ERC-721 tokens
Contracts that accept NFTs implement `IERC721Receiver`
This protects against sending NFTs to contracts that are unable to handle them
The same idea applies to transfers: `safeTransferFrom`

callout.text: For now remember: in normal NFT applications, `_safeMint` is generally the appropriate minting primitive.

slides.source: OpenZeppelin Docs — IERC721Receiver lets contracts accept NFTs safely via safeTransferFrom.

slides.title: Transfers & Approvals
slides.subtitle: Moving NFTs between owners  •  approve  •  setApprovalForAll

slides.title: Transferring an NFT
slides.intro: Creating an NFT is only one part — NFTs also need to move between owners.
points: Notice that ERC-721 transfers use a token ID
`safeTransferFrom` checks that a receiving contract can accept the NFT

left.heading: ERC-20
items: Moves an amount of fungible units

right.heading: ERC-721
items: Moves one specific token, identified by its token ID

callout.text: A very important comparison: ERC-20 moves amounts, ERC-721 moves specific token IDs.

slides.title: approve() — Permission for One NFT
slides.intro: In ERC-20, Alice could approve a spender for an amount. Because NFTs are unique, ERC-721 has two types of approval.

side.heading: approve(to, tokenId)
items: Grants permission for one specific NFT
The marketplace can now transfer NFT #10
Check it with `getApproved(10)`

side.heading: setApprovalForAll(op, true)
items: The operator can manage all of the owner's NFTs in this collection
Marketplaces use it to transfer an NFT when a sale occurs
Check it with `isApprovedForAll(Alice, Marketplace)`

callout.text: `approve(spender, tokenId)` → one NFT.   `setApprovalForAll(operator, true)` → all NFTs owned by the user for that ERC-721 contract.

slides.title: Metadata, tokenURI & IPFS
slides.subtitle: Where do the image, the name and the attributes come from?

slides.title: Where Does the Image Come From?
slides.intro: Now we understand ownership. But where do the image, the name, and attributes like strength, level or rarity come from? Answer: metadata.
points: `tokenURI(tokenId)` returns the location of a token's metadata
Wallets and marketplaces read that JSON to display the NFT

slides.title: Example NFT Metadata (JSON)
points: This is not Solidity — this is JSON metadata
`name` and `description` describe the NFT
`image` usually points to a file, for example on IPFS
`attributes` hold traits such as strength and level
Contract → `tokenURI(1)` → metadata → `image` → the NFT image

slides.title: Where Does the Metadata Live?
slides.intro: Storing large image files directly in normal Ethereum contract storage would generally be extremely expensive — so the contract usually references metadata using a URI.

cards.title: IPFS
cards.text: Content-addressed, decentralized file storage — commonly used for NFTs

cards.title: Arweave
cards.text: Decentralized storage designed for permanent data

cards.title: Web Server
cards.text: Simple to set up, but controlled by whoever runs the server

cards.title: On-chain
cards.text: Metadata generated by the contract itself

callout.text: IPFS is commonly used because it provides content-addressed decentralized file storage.
